Anuel AA Tells His Life Story, Walks Out of Interview After Tekashi 69 Questions (Full Interview)
recentItems.description:
Anuel AA sits down with VladTV for a rare first interview, tracing his journey from Carolina, Puerto Rico and the Sabana housing projects to becoming a pioneer of Latin trap. He opens up about his father’s Sony Music Puerto Rico background, early inspiration from Lil Wayne’s Tha Carter III, his grind with Rick Ross’ Maybach Music Group and Spiff TV, and the viral Bryant Myers remix that helped fuel the Spanish trap movement.

The conversation also covers Anuel’s 2016 weapons arrest, denied bail, 30-month prison sentence, missing his son, and the shocking rise that followed as Real Hasta La Muerte hit No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Latin Albums and broke Apple Music streaming records. He reflects on support from Daddy Yankee, Wisin, Yandel, his Billboard Latin Music Award win, Emmanuel, and working with Karol G. The interview takes a tense turn when Tekashi 6ix9ine, “BEBE,” “MALA,” and cooperation allegations come up—leading to Anuel walking out.

In this VladTV interview, Tito “TJ” Dominguez reflects on working around Carlos Escobar during the mid-1980s and witnessing the violent rise of Pablo Escobar’s Medellín Cartel. Discussing Escobar’s 1982 election to Colombia’s Chamber of Representatives with the Liberal Party, Tito addresses the fallout after Justice Minister Rodrigo Lara Bonilla exposed Pablo as a drug smuggler and was later killed by Escobar’s people.  

Tito describes his role as “contract work,” comparing himself to UPS while transporting duffel bags and insisting he was focused on money, not violence. He also offers a controversial view on cartel killings, saying many targets understood the risks of robbing or crossing traffickers. The conversation explores Pablo’s reputation, the ruthlessness of cousin Gustavo, and the deadly Medellín vs. Cali Cartel war that reshaped Colombia’s drug trade.

--------
In this VladTV interview, former Mexican Mafia member Rene “Boxer” Enriquez addresses a difficult and often misunderstood part of prison culture: sexuality, power, coercion, and status behind bars. Speaking with Vlad, Enriquez explains how attitudes varied across institutions and eras, including the prison slang around “pitching” and “catching,” and why one role could be tolerated while the other carried serious consequences in gang politics.

The conversation touches on figures and groups often discussed in California prison history, including Joe “Peg Leg” Morgan, Folsom Prison, the Mexican Mafia, Aryan Brotherhood, Nuestra Familia, and the Black Guerrilla Family. Enriquez also pushes back on Hollywood portrayals, specifically referencing American Me and Edward James Olmos, saying some prison rape scenes were exaggerated compared to what he personally witnessed.

A candid look at prison hierarchy, masculinity, gang rules, and the myths shaped by movies and street lore.
